extracted.intended_audience: laypersons and non-surgeon first-aid providers (general public, caretakers, responders without surgical training)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical first-aid instructions for laypeople covering recognition and emergency management of dislocations, dressings and bandages, poisoning (various kinds), food-borne illness, parasites, and basic preventive measures. Emphasizes immediate steps to take when skilled surgical attendance is unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiating dislocation from sprain and fracture
rubrics_metrics.description: Dislocated joint cannot be moved by the patient or another person except within narrow limits; a sprained joint can be moved (with pain) and has no mechanical obstacle. Fracture near a joint usually shows increased movement in a new direction; after reduction a dislocation stays in place whereas a reduced fracture will quickly resume its faulty position if unsupported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inability to move the joint and persistence of corrected position as key signs. Compare limb/joint movement and look for mechanical obstacle vs pain-only limitation. Check for abnormal increased movement in fractures.

rubrics_metrics.name: General instruction: seek skilled surgical attendance when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructions provided are not to be followed if skilled surgical attendance can be secured; they are intended solely for those not so fortunately situated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize obtaining professional care; follow lay instructions only when no surgeon is available. Avoid attempting reductions or procedures beyond your skill if professional help can be obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dislocation of the jaw — recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Jaw dislocation may be bilateral (chin projecting, mouth open and cannot be closed, lower front teeth jut beyond upper) or unilateral (chin pushed toward uninjured side, face appears twisted, depression in front of ear on injured side and prominence on opposite side).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect chin projection, mouth openness and asymmetry. Note depressions/prominences near ear; assess pain and inability to close mouth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dislocation of the jaw — reduction methods and aftercare
rubrics_metrics.description: Two methods: (1) cork method — place a good-sized cork far back between back teeth of upper and lower jaws and get patient to bite to pry jaw back; (2) operator method — protect thumbs (bandage or leather gloves), assistant steadies head, operator presses downward and backward on back teeth with thumbs while forefingers raise chin; when jaw slips into place maintain with bandage around head under chin for a week and feed patient on liquids through a tube.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect thumbs to avoid injury. After reduction, immobilize for a week and avoid opening mouth—feed liquids via tube. Do not attempt complex maneuvers if skilled help is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dislocation of the shoulder — recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Most common adult dislocation: head of humerus slips downward (or inward and forward). Injured shoulder loses fullness, looks flatter; arm held with elbow away from side and arm slopes inward; patient cannot place hand of injured arm on opposite shoulder or touch side with elbow at right angle without great pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare appearance with uninjured shoulder; note loss of fullness and characteristic arm position; inability to make certain movements indicates dislocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dislocation of the shoulder — reduction (Stimson's method) and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Stimson's method: patient lies on injured side on a canvas cot raised from floor so arm hangs through a hole; attach a 10-pound weight to wrist and allow gradual traction (often reduces within ~6 minutes). Alternative: patient supine, operator sits with stockinged foot against patient's side under injured armpit and pulls the arm outward while assistant lifts head of humerus in armpit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gradual traction with weight for painless reduction when suitable. If reduction does not occur easily, stop further attempts. If dislocation is several days old or patient is very muscular, a surgeon and anesthesia (ether) may be required. After reduction, bandage arm to side and use sling for about ten days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit attempts at reduction and when to involve surgeon
rubrics_metrics.description: If the arm does not go into place easily by a method, it is unwise to continue further attempts. If shoulder has been dislocated several days or patient is very muscular, surgeon with ether may be necessary. A skillful surgeon can sometimes reduce a dislocation even weeks after occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repeated forceful attempts that could cause further injury. Seek surgical assistance in delayed or difficult cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dislocation of the elbow — recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Common in children after fall on outstretched hand. Elbow displaced backward; joint swollen and held slightly bent; tip of elbow projects at back of joint; at front the distance between wrist and bend of elbow is less than sound arm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare three bony landmarks on each elbow (two prominences at sides and tip of elbow) by touch to confirm displacement. Differentiate from fracture by noting if deformity recurs after release (fracture) vs stays reduced (dislocation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dislocation of the elbow — reduction and aftercare
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce by bending forearm backward to straight or slightly past straight, assistant holds arm above elbow, operator grasps forearm below elbow and pulls with great force away from assistant, then suddenly bend elbow forward to right angle so bones slip into place. After treatment, apply a well-padded right-angled tin splint bound with plaster and bandage for two to three weeks; remove splint every few days to gently move elbow to prevent stiffness and then reapply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strong traction followed by sudden flexion to reduce. Post-reduction care includes immobilization in right-angled splint for 2–3 weeks with periodic gentle movement to prevent stiffness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dislocation of the hip — recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs commonly in males 15–45 from external violence. In ordinary form patient stands on sound leg with body bent forward; injured leg greatly shortened with toes turned inward and foot crossing over instep of sound foot; injured limb cannot be moved outward, may be bent forward; walking impossible; pain and deformity evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate from fracture of hip (more common in elderly) which shows less shortening, toes often turned out, and some weight-bearing possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dislocation of the hip — reduction (Stimson traction and alternatives) and aftercare
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplest treatment (Stimson): sling patient vertically by sheet under armpits so feet dangle ~1 foot from floor; attach 10–15 lb weight to foot to draw bone down into socket within 10–15 minutes. Alternative prone table position with assistant holding uninjured leg and another applying a 5–10 lb sandbag at knee flexure while moving ankle gently side to side. After reduction, patient should stay in bed 1–2 weeks then gradually use crutches for ~2 more weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use traction weights to achieve gradual reduction. Adjust weight to patient muscle strength. Follow with bed rest and progressive mobilization on crutches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sterilized gauze as primary surgical dressing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sterilized gauze (cheese cloth boiled in alkaline solution and rinsed) is the chief surgical dressing. Sterilize by baking (in tin boxes or wrapped in cloth until browning), steaming (Arnold sterilizer), or boiling (for wet application). Cut gauze into hand-sized pieces before sterilizing; keep sealed until use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid opening sterilized packages until use; inspect small test piece during baking to gauge progress. Carbolized, borated, and corrosive-sublimate gauze have little special value. Sterilized gauze may be purchased from surgical suppliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absorbent cotton use and sterilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Absorbent cotton should be sterilized if used on raw surfaces; it mats down and may stick to wounds so is less useful than gauze for dressings. Boiled cotton torn into egg-sized balls is useful as sponges for cleaning wounds. Sheet wadding useful to cover splints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sterilize cotton by boiling for 15 minutes when using as sponges. Prefer gauze for primary dressings; use cotton primarily for sponges or padding under splints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wet antiseptic surgical dressings — preparation and covering
rubrics_metrics.description: Wet antiseptic dressings are made by soaking gauze in solutions of carbolic acid (½ teaspoonful to 1 pint hot water), then covering with oiled material such as oil silk, rubber dam, paraffin paper, or heavily oiled brown wrapping paper when better material is unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wet antiseptic dressings for inflamed wounds not healing well. Ensure outer cover is waterproof to keep dressing moist and antiseptic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bandage materials, sizes, and rolling technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Cotton cloth (bleached or unbleached) and gauze are commonly employed. A bandage must be rolled before application. Limb bandage: ~2.5 inches wide and 8 yards long; finger bandage: ¾ inch wide and 3 yards long. Roll by rolling on itself to the size of a finger then roll down the limb using the palm while holding the loose end taut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare bandages of correct width/length for body parts. Rolling before application avoids handling/contamination. Use gauze for novice-friendly softer bandaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bandaging techniques: spiral reversed, figure-of-eight, T-bandage, triangular bandage
rubrics_metrics.description: Two limb bandages: figure-of-eight and spiral reversed. Always begin at lower extremity and approach body. Make circular turns, then spiral up reversing each encirclement. T-bandage used for crotch or forehead (ends put about body and brought between thighs/over head). Triangular bandage (large handkerchief folded diagonally) is invaluable in emergencies for dressing wounds or fractures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reverse bandage securely to prevent slipping. Use triangular bandage for improvised slings/splints and as general-purpose emergency bandage. Reference illustrations for specific applications (thumb spica, groin spica, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: First Aid general rules for poisoning (First Aid Rule 1–3)
rubrics_metrics.description: First Aid Rule 1: Send at once for physician. Rule 2: Empty stomach with emetic. Rule 3: Give antidote. In most poisonings emetics and purgatives do the most good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act immediately; while awaiting physician, prioritize stomach emptying and antidote administration where appropriate. Use emetics/purgatives as first-line lay interventions when indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unknown poisons — immediate lay treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Act at once; give two teaspoonfuls of chalk (or whiting/whitewash scrapings) mixed with a wineglass of water. Beat four eggs in a glass of milk, add a tablespoonful of whisky, and give at once. Be prepared to perform artificial respiration if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin general neutralizing/stomach-emptying measures immediately; identify poison afterward to tailor further therapy. Do not delay initial steps waiting for identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acid poisoning — specific antidotes and supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Carbolic acid: give a tablespoonful of alcohol or wineglass of whisky/brandy; or a tablespoonful of castor oil, half pint sweet oil, and a pint of milk; put to bed and apply hot-water bottles. Nitric/oxalic: chalk/lime/whitewash (1 tsp in ¼ glass water), one tablespoonful castor oil, half pint sweet oil, rectal injection of 1 tbsp whisky in 2 tbsp water. Sulphuric: soapsuds half glass and a pint of milk. Other acids: limewater or two tsp aromatic spirit of ammonia diluted, plus castor oil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the antidote/neutralizer to type of acid. Provide oils and soothing agents for corrosives; use alcohol for carbolic poisoning. Provide warmth and rest as supportive care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alkali poisoning — antidotes and supportive care
rubrics_metrics.description: For ammonia, potash, lye, caustic soda, washing soda: give half glass vinegar mixed with half glass water; juice of four lemons in two glasses of water; one teaspoonful castor oil in half glass of olive oil. If prostrated, give a tablespoonful of whisky in a quarter glass of hot water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutralize alkalies with weak acids (vinegar/lemon). Provide castor/olive oil to protect mucosa and support, and stimulants if prostration occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metal poisoning — recognition and antidotes (arsenic, copper, mercury, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arsenic: intense GI pain, vomiting/ bloody purging — best antidote hydrated sesquioxide of iron (2 ounces) given tablespoon every quarter hour in ½ glass water; or limewater then mustard teaspoon. Copper: one tablespoon mustard in warm water, then whites of three eggs and a pint milk after vomiting. Mercury (corrosive sublimate): whites of four eggs per suspected grain; induce vomiting with mustard or powdered ipecac. Silver nitrate: two tsp table salt in two glasses hot water, then castor oil. Phosphorus: teaspoon mustard then gum arabic after vomiting; give Epsom salts hour later; DO NOT GIVE OIL. Antimony: 30 grains powdered ipecac in wineglass water, strong tea or oak bark infusion, two tsp whisky in hot water, warmers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specific chemical antidote where named; induce vomiting when appropriate; avoid oils for some poisons (phosphorus). Seek pharmacy/druggist for hydrated iron for arsenic if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narcotic poisoning — general approach (stomach pump, emetics, stimulants, respiratory support)
rubrics_metrics.description: For narcotics (aconite, belladonna, camphor, digitalis, etc.) use stomach pump at once; if unavailable, siphon with rubber tube and funnel or give 30 grains powdered ipecac in wineglass water followed by warm water, then strong hot coffee and castor oil. Keep patient awake by rubbing, keep warm; give stimulants (whisky) if prostration. For opium/morphine give ammonia inhalation, permanganate of potash, rectal injection of black coffee, rubbing and artificial respiration if needed, and tincture of belladonna to assist breathing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empty stomach early when possible. Maintain respiration and circulation with stimulants, rubs, hot-water bottles; avoid exhausting the patient by walking; use hypodermics (strychnine) only when skilled or indicated (see specific sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcohol and sedative poisoning — stomach emptying and stimulants
rubrics_metrics.description: For alcohol: use stomach pump or ipecac (30 grains powdered ipecac), then 30 drops aromatic spirit of ammonia in a wineglass water every half hour until pulse is full and rapid; apply cold to head and heat to extremities. For chloral and sleeping mixtures: stomach pump, or ipecac, then 2 tsp whisky in half glass hot water, sulphate of strychnine hypodermically 1/20 grain every 2–3 hours until roused; rubbing and hot-water bottles; follow artificial respiration if breathing ceases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stimulants and countermeasures to restore circulation and respiration. Use hypodermic strychnine only when available and indicated; artificial respiration per suffocation protocol if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific treatments for opium, tobacco, nux vomica, cocaine, phenacetin, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Opium: stomach pump or ipecac, inhaled ammonia, permanganate doses, rectal coffee, rubbing, artificial respiration, tincture of belladonna (30 drops hourly). Tobacco: ipecac, whisky. Nux vomica/strychnine: ipecac, then chloral (20 grains) and bromide sodium (30 grains) rectally/internally; if convulsions give chloroform on handkerchief. Cocaine: whisky doses, hypodermic strychnine (1/30 grain) to maintain pulse, hot-water bottles. Phenacetin/acetanilid: whisky; if heart weak, tincture of digitalis or digitalin (hypodermic preferred).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow poison-specific recipes; use stimulants for CNS depressants; use soporifics/anticonvulsants where indicated; avoid exhaustion of patient; attempt gastric emptying early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food poisoning — immediate objectives and first aid rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives: rid patient of poison (induce repeated vomiting), empty bowels (warm soapsuds enema), support heart and rally nerve force (teaspoon whisky in tablespoon hot water every half hour as needed), keep patient warm with hot-water bottles and blankets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induce vomiting with repeated tepid water with mustard (½ tsp) or finger in throat if necessary; use enemas for bowel emptying; give stimulants and supportive care after evacuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foods and conditions commonly causing bacterial food poisoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Offending foods include meats, fish, shellfish, milk, cheese, ice cream, uncooked blood of river eel, fermented/canned/putrefied fish, sausages with putrefied ingredients, imperfectly cured bacon, putrefied cheese, improperly handled milk, ice cream fermented before freezing, mouldy corn meal and bread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize likely sources by recent common meal among affected persons. Suspect food poisoning when several people have similar symptoms hours after eating same food.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infected food and milk — prevention and treatment implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Food (meat, oysters, milk) contaminated with disease germs may transmit disease if eaten raw; cooking to boiling point provides comparative safety but toxins may remain. Milk should be kept cool, never left uncovered, and when in doubt should be heated to 160°F for 10 minutes (pasteurization) before giving to children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize prevention via hygiene in dairying and during transport; in households, cool and cover milk and pasteurize doubtful milk for children. Treatment must be disease-specific if a transmissible infection is suspected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food parasites prevention and tapeworm home remedy when physician unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevention: thorough cooking of meats (especially pork and beef) prevents entrance of living parasites (trichina, tapeworm). Tapeworm (from 'measly' meat): after 24-hour fast, take crushed pumpkin seed (2 oz child, 4 oz adult) soaked overnight on empty stomach; child mixed with syrup/honey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize prevention by cooking; use pumpkin seed home remedy only when no physician available and follow fasting instructions. Successful tapeworm treatment should be supervised by physician if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trichiniasis — recognition and lack of cure; prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Trichiniasis from raw/partly cooked pork causes nausea, vomiting, diarrhea within ~2 days, later muscle stiffness, swelling of face/extremities, sweating, hoarseness, breathing difficulty, bronchitis, pneumonia. There is no treatment; many nonfatal cases may be mistaken for rheumatism or pneumonia may result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevention via thorough cooking of pork. Recognize systemic signs and seek medical care; do not rely on lay cures as there is no established treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potato poisoning recognition and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Solanine in sprouting potatoes causes violent vomiting, diarrhea, and inflammation of stomach/bowels. Careful peeling of sprouting potatoes and removal of eyes will lessen or obviate danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid eating sprouting or green potatoes; peel thoroughly and remove eyes. Be aware this is a rare form of food poisoning but can occur unexpectedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle: use stomach pump or siphon early in poisoning
rubrics_metrics.description: For many poisons (narcotics, alcohols, some metals) use the stomach pump at once; if pump not available, siphon with rubber tube and funnel, or induce vomiting with powdered ipecac (30 grains in a wineglass of water) and follow with warm water as vomiting proceeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early gastric decontamination is emphasized repeatedly. Use mechanical methods when available; otherwise induce emesis promptly. Keep patient under supervision; manage fluids and warmth.
